catalog_quote: 3.3. Syllable and Word Structure. The structure of the vernacular word is similar to mod. Khmer. ... 3.3.3. The Dissyllable. The dissyllable, invariably iambic, consists of a stressed monosyllable or subdissyllable with an unstressed presyllable of the shapes Crə- and Cəɴ-. In these formulæ C continues to represent any allowable consonant. This is followed in the first case by /-rə/, in the second case by /-əɴ/, in which ɴ represents a nasal frequently but not always assimilating to the initial of the main syllable. Examples: 16. travāṅ /trəbaŋ/ ‘reservoir’ 17. cramuḥ /crəmʊh/ ‘nose’ 18. prasir /prəsiːr/ ‘writing’ 19. caṅvāt /cəŋwat/ ‘delimited terrain’ 20. kañjuḥ /kəɲɟʊh/ ‘dung’ 21. randaḥ /rəndah/ ‘lightning’ 22. paṃroḥ /ɓəmrɔh/ ‘trash’ 3.3.4. Compounds. The above are the characteristic wordforms of vernacular Old Khmer. Other words, relatively few in number, show these same forms gro…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Old Khmer native words are monosyllables (CVF), 'subdissyllables' (CCVF, phonetically mono- to sesquisyllabic with a weightless juncture vowel) or dissyllables; dissyllables are always iambic: the final (main) syllable carries the stress and the presyllable (Crə- or Cəɴ-, with reduced /ə/) is unstressed. Hence word stress falls on the final syllable. This is a reconstructed phonology for an epigraphic language, modelled on modern Khmer.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; presyllables and juncture vowels are described as unstressed / without phonological weight.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds (few) group these word shapes together (3.3.4); loanwords 'generally follow the structure of the source language' though many Sanskrit/Prakrit loans are assimilated to the Khmer canonical forms (3.3.5); Jenner 2009 (PL 597 p. xvi, PL 598 p. xi) adds that in Indic loans final -a and suffixes like -ana were dropped and Sanskrit penult stress shifted, with unstressed a > [ə]. Authors flag the whole system as 'a reconstructed system, plausible enough but liable to modification' (p. 6).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word / wordform structure of vernacular vocabulary); statement concerns dissyllabic words, monosyllables trivially stressed; no phrase-level prosody discussed. Same statement, with stress marks on the final syllable in transcriptions (/ɓəmˈnɔːŋ/, /trəˈkaːl/), in Jenner 2009 Dictionary of pre-Angkorian Khmer p. xvi and Dictionary of Angkorian Khmer p. xii (both saved).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Old Khmer as a whole (pre-Angkorian 612-802 and Angkorian 802-1431 'dialectal variants'), i.e. Glottolog oldk1249 [qok]; the phonology is explicitly a reconstruction for an epigraphic language, modelled partly on modern Khmer (khme1253/cent1989). Note Glottolog's series number 'Pacific Linguistics 623' is wrong; the volume is PL 611.

sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology, sec. 3.3.3 p. 8: 'The dissyllable, invariably iambic, consists of a stressed monosyllable or subdissyllable with an unstressed presyllable of the shapes Crə- and Cəɴ-.' Also p. 6: /ə/ is 'the unstressed allophone of /ɤ/ occurring in presyllables and Indic loans'; fn. 3 p. 8: sesquisyllabic words have 'a light initial syllable with no phonological weight'. I.e. stress on the word-final (main) syllable.

sources.note: Introduction p. xii: 'The phonological dissyllable consists of a stressed CVF main syllable with an unstressed presyllable of either of two forms: Cəɴ- (laṃṅāc /ləmˈŋaːc/ withdrawal) or Crə- (trakāl /trəˈkaːl/ to be high).' p. xi: /ə/ 'the unstressed allophone of /ɤ/'.
